name: Reorder stock on measured lead times and read supplier confirmations with Gmail, Sheets and AI

parameters.content:
## Reorder stock on measured lead times and read supplier confirmations with Gmail, Sheets and AI

### How it works

1. The sheet is audited before anything is ordered from it: deliveries past their date, receipts booked short, and stock the count, receipts and sales do not explain.
2. Demand is measured per product over the days it was in stock. A week out of stock is not a week of no demand, and one bulk order is not the new normal.
3. Lead time is the 80th percentile of your receipts, one sample per delivery, not per line, or the quoted figure when history is thin.
4. The reorder point covers demand over that lead time plus the review period, with safety stock for how much both of them vary. Goods already on order count against it.
5. One purchase order per supplier, rounded to their minimum and pack size, capped by shelf life, and held under their minimum order value unless a line runs out first.
6. Confirmations are read as they arrive. One short or late enough to arrive after the shelf empties goes to the buyer instead.

### Setup steps

- [ ] Connect Gmail, Google Sheets and OpenAI credentials.
- [ ] Create one sheet with six tabs: Products, Sales, Stockouts, Purchase orders, Suppliers, Reorder log.
- [ ] Put the sheet ID and your addresses in both Set nodes: the triggers never run together.
- [ ] Check the service level, the cover and the approval limit in Set Reorder Policy.

### Customization

Every threshold is in a Set node. The demand estimate, the lead times and the order quantities are one Code node.

## Start the replenishment run

Seven in the morning, Monday to Friday. **Set Reorder Policy** is the only node in this branch you edit: the sheet ID, two addresses, and every threshold the planner reads.

## Read the stock and outages

Products carries the shelf, the pack sizes and the last physical count. Stockouts carries the days a line could not be sold at all, and without it a sold-out month reads as a month of no demand.

## Read the sales history

One row per sale. Ninety days of it is enough to measure a rate; the **Aggregate** node folds the read into a single item, because a Sheets node runs once for every item it is handed.

## Read the orders in flight

Everything ordered and not yet received. It is what stops the run asking for stock that is already on a lorry, and it is where the lead times are measured from.

## Read suppliers and the log

Supplier terms - minimum order, pack, order days, quoted lead time - and our own log. The log is how the run knows what it said yesterday, and to whom.

## Audit the books first

The sheet, read against itself before anything is ordered from it. It always returns at least one item: a node that returns nothing would stop the reorder run underneath it.

## Chase the late deliveries

One email per supplier rather than per line, and only every few days: the log above says when we last wrote. Overdue orders and short deliveries go in the same message.

parameters.message:
=Hello{{ $json.contact_name ? ' ' + $json.contact_name : '' }},

Our records show the following outstanding against orders placed with you.

{{ $json.detail }}

Could you send a date for each of these, or tell us what has gone wrong with them? We plan the next order round them, so a realistic date is worth more to us than an optimistic one.
parameters.subject: ={{ $json.subject_line }}

parameters.content:
## Suspend a suspect stock record

The count, plus receipts, minus sales, is not what the stock column says. The row is marked, and nothing is ordered against it until somebody has been to the shelf.

parameters.subject: =Stock records that do not add up: {{ $json.rows.length }} line(s)

parameters.content:
## Plan the reorder quantities

The node this template exists for: demand per sellable day, lead time from our own receipts, safety stock, and one order per supplier. The loop then takes them one at a time.

## Ask the buyer about big orders

Over the limit, a supplier nothing has ever arrived from, or a price that has moved: the buyer gets the arithmetic and three days. A refusal is logged as plainly as an order.

parameters.subject: =Approve {{ $json.po_number }}? {{ $json.currency }} {{ $json.order_value }} to {{ $json.supplier_name }}

parameters.message:
=Hello{{ $('Loop Over Supplier Orders').first().json.contact_name ? ' ' + $('Loop Over Supplier Orders').first().json.contact_name : '' }},

Please supply the following against purchase order {{ $('Loop Over Supplier Orders').first().json.po_number }}.

{{ $('Loop Over Supplier Orders').first().json.table }}

We would like it with us by {{ $('Loop Over Supplier Orders').first().json.expected_on }}.

Reply to this email to confirm, leaving {{ $('Loop Over Supplier Orders').first().json.po_number }} in the subject line, and say the quantity and the date you can actually do. A short or late confirmation read this morning is worth more to us than a full one that turns out not to be true.
parameters.subject: ={{ $('Loop Over Supplier Orders').first().json.subject_line }}

parameters.content:
## Send the purchase order

One order per supplier, carrying every line under its reorder point. **Split Out Order Lines** turns that order back into rows, one per line, for the sheet.

parameters.message:
=Hello{{ $json.contact_name ? ' ' + $json.contact_name : '' }},

Please supply the following against purchase order {{ $json.po_number }}.

{{ $json.table }}

We would like it with us by {{ $json.expected_on }}.

Reply to this email to confirm, leaving {{ $json.po_number }} in the subject line, and say the quantity and the date you can actually do. A short or late confirmation read this morning is worth more to us than a full one that turns out not to be true.
parameters.subject: ={{ $json.subject_line }}

parameters.content:
## Write the order into Sheets

The pipeline is written before anything reads it again: each line lands in Purchase orders with the demand it was ordered against and the day the shelf empties. The reply branch compares against those two.

assignments.name: decided_by
assignments.value: ={{ $('Loop Over Supplier Orders').first().json.action === 'approve' ? $('Set Reorder Policy').first().json.buyer_email : 'the reorder policy' }}

parameters.content:
## Hold, flag, or do nothing

Under the supplier's minimum, or their order day is Thursday: it waits, and tomorrow's run adds to it. What needs a person is one email, not one per line.

parameters.subject: ={{ $json.subject_line }}

parameters.content:
## Catch the supplier replies

Every reply, read within fifteen minutes. **Read Open Orders for Reply** runs once however many emails arrived, so two replies in one poll do not read the tab twice.

filters.q: in:inbox -from:me newer_than:30d subject:(PO OR order OR purchase OR delivery)

parameters.content:
## Read the reply with AI

The thread under a reply is our own email, and a model asked what was confirmed will read our numbers back to us. It is cut off before the model sees it.

options.systemPromptTemplate:
You are reading a supplier's reply to a purchase order.

Copy what they wrote. Do not infer, do not calculate, do not decide whether it is acceptable: somebody else does that, and they need your reading of the words rather than your opinion of them.

The text you are given is only what this person typed today. If a quantity, a date or a price is not in it, return an empty string - a blank is handled downstream, an invented number is a delivery nobody is expecting.

Dates are copied in the writer's own format.

attributes.name: po_number
attributes.description: The purchase order number this reply is about, copied exactly. Empty string if the text does not contain one.

attributes.name: sku
attributes.description: The product code the reply is about, copied exactly. Empty string if it names none.

attributes.name: confirmed_quantity
attributes.description: The quantity they say they will supply, as a plain number. Empty string if they give no quantity.

attributes.name: confirmed_date
attributes.description: The date they say it will be delivered or shipped, copied exactly as written. Empty string if they give none.

attributes.name: confirmed_unit_price
attributes.description: The unit price they quote, as a plain number. Empty string if they quote none.

attributes.name: summary
attributes.description: One sentence saying what this supplier is telling us, in plain words.

parameters.content:
## Compare it with the order

Not whether anything changed, but whether the change reaches past the day the shelf empties. The order line carries the demand it was ordered against, so this is arithmetic and not a second forecast.

## Accept the confirmed order

A confirmation that still lands in time takes the new date and the new quantity. The pipeline then shows what is really coming, so tomorrow's run can make up the difference elsewhere.

## Escalate a late or short order

Short, later than the day the shelf empties, or dearer than the order: the line is flagged at risk and the buyer gets the numbers, rather than the sheet quietly taking them.

parameters.subject: =At risk: {{ $json.po_number }} {{ $json.sku }} ({{ $json.days_uncovered }} day(s) uncovered)

parameters.content:
## Leave the rest to a person

A confirmation for an order that does not exist, or for a four-line order without saying which line. An out-of-office ends at the No Operation node and changes nothing.

parameters.subject: =Supplier reply needs you: {{ $json.from }}

parameters.content:
## Report a workflow failure

A third entry point, firing only when a run errors. A replenishment workflow that fails quietly looks exactly like a month in which nothing needed ordering.

parameters.subject: =Replenishment workflow failed: {{ $json.execution.id }}
